claim: Wildtype Dictyostelium amoebae feed on bacteria.
source: Wildtype Dictyostelium amoebae feed on bacteria, but for decades laboratory work has relied on axenic mutants that can also grow on liquid media.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Dictyostelium biology.

claim: Laboratory work with Dictyostelium has relied on axenic mutants that can grow on liquid media for decades.
source: Wildtype Dictyostelium amoebae feed on bacteria, but for decades laboratory work has relied on axenic mutants that can also grow on liquid media.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about laboratory practices.

claim: The gene underlying the axenic growth phenotype encodes the RasGAP Neurofibromin (NF1).
source: This gene encodes the RasGAP Neurofibromin (NF1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, identified through forward genetics and genome sequencing.

claim: Loss of NF1 enables axenic growth by increasing fluid uptake.
source: Loss of NF1 enables axenic growth by increasing fluid uptake.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing NF1 mutants to wildtype cells.

claim: NF1 mutants form outsized macropinosomes.
source: Mutants form outsized macropinosomes which are promoted by greater Ras and PI3K activity at sites of endocytosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data.

claim: Outsized macropinosomes in NF1 mutants are promoted by greater Ras and PI3K activity at sites of endocytosis.
source: Mutants form outsized macropinosomes which are promoted by greater Ras and PI3K activity at sites of endocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by reporter imaging showing increased Ras and PI3K activity at macropinocytosis sites.

claim: NF1 mutants can ingest larger-than-normal particles using phagocytosis.
source: Relatedly, NF1 mutants can ingest larger-than-normal particles using phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing uptake of larger beads and yeast cells.

claim: An NF1 reporter is recruited to nascent macropinosomes.
source: An NF1 reporter is recruited to nascent macropinosomes, suggesting that NF1 limits their size by locally inhibiting Ras signalling.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing GFP-tagged NF1 localization.

claim: NF1 limits macropinosome size by locally inhibiting Ras signalling.
source: An NF1 reporter is recruited to nascent macropinosomes, suggesting that NF1 limits their size by locally inhibiting Ras signalling.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the localization data and the known GAP activity of NF1.

claim: This is the first time NF1 has been linked with macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
source: Our results link NF1 with macropinocytosis and phagocytosis for the first time, and we propose that NF1 evolved in early phagotrophs to spatially modulate Ras activity, thereby constraining and shaping their feeding structures.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: NF1 evolved in early phagotrophs to spatially modulate Ras activity, thereby constraining and shaping their feeding structures.
source: Our results link NF1 with macropinocytosis and phagocytosis for the first time, and we propose that NF1 evolved in early phagotrophs to spatially modulate Ras activity, thereby constraining and shaping their feeding structures.
evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary hypothesis based on the functional data and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: A wide range of unicellular eukaryotes grow by phagotrophy.
source: A wide range of unicellular eukaryotes grow in this way, suggesting that it is extremely old in evolutionary terms (Stanier, 1970; Cavalier-Smith, 2002; Yutin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phagotrophy is extremely old in evolutionary terms.
source: A wide range of unicellular eukaryotes grow in this way, suggesting that it is extremely old in evolutionary terms (Stanier, 1970; Cavalier-Smith, 2002; Yutin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phagocytosis is typically used by unicellular eukaryotes to engulf solid particles.
source: Typically phagocytosis is used by these organisms to engulf solid particles (Metchnikoff, 1892), and nutrients are then extracted from them by lysosomal degradation (De Duve and Wattiaux, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nutrients are extracted from phagocytosed particles by lysosomal degradation.
source: Typically phagocytosis is used by these organisms to engulf solid particles (Metchnikoff, 1892), and nutrients are then extracted from them by lysosomal degradation (De Duve and Wattiaux, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Animal cells and amoebae ingest solid material using F-actin driven projections of their plasma membrane.
source: Animal cells and amoebae ingest solid material using F-actin driven projections of their plasma membrane, forming pseudopodia and ultimately cup- or crown-shaped ruffles that enclose adhered particles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of phagocytosis.

claim: Macropinocytosis is a process by which cells internalize bulk fluid without the guidance of a particle.
source: These cells can also internalise bulk fluid without the guidance of a particle using a closely related process, macropinocytosis (Swanson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phagocytosis and macropinocytosis are controlled by a large set of cytoskeletal and membrane-associated regulators, notably small G proteins.
source: Phagocytosis and macropinocytosis are controlled using a large set of cytoskeletal and membrane-associated regulators, notably a variety of small G proteins (Bar-Sagi and Feramisco, 1986; Ridley et al., 1992; Peters et al., 1995; Cox et al., 1997; Martínez-Martín et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oncogenes such as Src and PI3K have been linked with regulation of phagocytosis and macropinocytosis.
source: Oncogenes such as Src and phosphatidylinositide 3′-kinase (PI3K) have also been linked with regulation of these processes (Araki et al., 1996; Veithen et al., 1996; Buczynski et al., 1997; Amyere et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In amoebae, growth and endocytosis have obvious connections since phagocytosed material supplies essentially all their nutrients.
source: In amoebae, growth and endocytosis have obvious connections since phagocytosed material supplies essentially all their nutrients; in contrast vertebrates are specialised to digest food extracellularly in the gut, and so links are less apparent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about amoebae biology.

claim: Vertebrates are specialized to digest food extracellularly in the gut.
source: In amoebae, growth and endocytosis have obvious connections since phagocytosed material supplies essentially all their nutrients; in contrast vertebrates are specialised to digest food extracellularly in the gut, and so links are less apparent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vertebrate biology.

claim: Large-scale endocytosis is extremely important in immune cells.
source: However, large-scale endocytosis is extremely important in immune cells (Metchnikoff, 1892; Norbury et al., 1995; Sallusto et al., 1995), while tumour cells, released from the normal constraints on growth and proliferation, can display pronounced macropinocytotic or phagocytotic uptake (Lewis, 1937; Montcourrier et al., 1994), and can feed by ingesting extracellular protein (Commisso et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tumor cells can display pronounced macropinocytotic or phagocytotic uptake.
source: However, large-scale endocytosis is extremely important in immune cells (Metchnikoff, 1892; Norbury et al., 1995; Sallusto et al., 1995), while tumour cells, released from the normal constraints on growth and proliferation, can display pronounced macropinocytotic or phagocytotic uptake (Lewis, 1937; Montcourrier et al., 1994), and can feed by ingesting extracellular protein (Commisso et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tumor cells can feed by ingesting extracellular protein.
source: However, large-scale endocytosis is extremely important in immune cells (Metchnikoff, 1892; Norbury et al., 1995; Sallusto et al., 1995), while tumour cells, released from the normal constraints on growth and proliferation, can display pronounced macropinocytotic or phagocytotic uptake (Lewis, 1937; Montcourrier et al., 1994), and can feed by ingesting extracellular protein (Commisso et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There are clear similarities between large-scale endocytosis in animal cells and amoebae.
source: While there are clear similarities between large-scale endocytosis in animal cells and amoebae, neither the regulatory architecture nor evolutionary contexts are adequately understood.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The regulatory architecture of large-scale endocytosis is not adequately understood.
source: While there are clear similarities between large-scale endocytosis in animal cells and amoebae, neither the regulatory architecture nor evolutionary contexts are adequately understood.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The evolutionary contexts of large-scale endocytosis are not adequately understood.
source: While there are clear similarities between large-scale endocytosis in animal cells and amoebae, neither the regulatory architecture nor evolutionary contexts are adequately understood.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Dictyostelium feeds primarily on bacteria in the wild.
source: Phagotrophic microorganisms can be difficult to study in the laboratory because of their requirement for other organisms as food. This can be overcome if cells can be cultured axenically ('a-xenic' indicating the absence of organisms of another species): in some cases, such as the social amoeba Dictyostelium, which feeds primarily on bacteria in the wild (Vuillemin, 1903), strains were gradually adapted to growth in complex liquid broth, and ultimately in chemically defined media (Sussman and Sussman, 1967; Watts and Ashworth, 1970; Franke and Kessin, 1977; Watts, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dictyostelium strains were gradually adapted to growth in complex liquid broth and ultimately in chemically defined media.
source: Phagotrophic microorganisms can be difficult to study in the laboratory because of their requirement for other organisms as food. This can be overcome if cells can be cultured axenically ('a-xenic' indicating the absence of organisms of another species): in some cases, such as the social amoeba Dictyostelium, which feeds primarily on bacteria in the wild (Vuillemin, 1903), strains were gradually adapted to growth in complex liquid broth, and ultimately in chemically defined media (Sussman and Sussman, 1967; Watts and Ashworth, 1970; Franke and Kessin, 1977; Watts, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The process of adapting Dictyostelium to axenic growth involved the selection of mutants that display increased rates of macropinocytosis.
source: This process involved the selection of mutants that display increased rates of macropinocytosis (Watts and Ashworth, 1970; Loomis, 1971; Hacker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two important mutations, axeA and axeB, were identified by linkage analysis as being necessary for robust axenic growth.
source: Two important mutations, axeA and axeB, were identified by linkage analysis as being necessary for robust axenic growth (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b), but only the latter is strictly required (Clarke and Kayman, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only axeB is strictly required for axenic growth.
source: Two important mutations, axeA and axeB, were identified by linkage analysis as being necessary for robust axenic growth (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b), but only the latter is strictly required (Clarke and Kayman, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Axenic mutant strains have been very widely used for over 40 years.
source: Although these axenic mutant strains have been very widely used for over 40 years, the genetic basis of their growth has remained mysterious, since the mutations could not be precisely mapped.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about laboratory practices.

claim: The genetic basis of axenic growth has remained mysterious because the mutations could not be precisely mapped.
source: Although these axenic mutant strains have been very widely used for over 40 years, the genetic basis of their growth has remained mysterious, since the mutations could not be precisely mapped.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the historical state of knowledge.

claim: A forward genetic approach was used to identify mutations that promote axenic growth in Dictyostelium discoideum using whole genome sequencing.
source: We used a forward genetic approach to identify mutations that promote axenic growth in Dictyostelium discoideum using whole genome sequencing.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The Dictyostelium orthologue of NF1 is a key regulator of both macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
source: We found that the Dictyostelium orthologue of the Ras GTPase activating protein (RasGAP) Neurofibromin (NF1), a tumour suppressor that is mutated in the genetic disorder Neurofibromatosis type 1 (Xu et al., 1990), is a key regulator of both macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: NF1 is a tumor suppressor that is mutated in the genetic disorder Neurofibromatosis type 1.
source: We found that the Dictyostelium orthologue of the Ras GTPase activating protein (RasGAP) Neurofibromin (NF1), a tumour suppressor that is mutated in the genetic disorder Neurofibromatosis type 1 (Xu et al., 1990), is a key regulator of both macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Wildtype D. discoideum cells arrest their growth and ultimately die when cultured in HL5 growth medium after washing free of food bacteria.
source: To generate fresh axenic strains for sequencing, we cultured wildtype D. discoideum cells in HL5 growth medium after washing them free of food bacteria. This medium supports the growth of axenic strains such as Ax2 and AX4, but wildtype cells arrest their growth and ultimately die.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: HL5 medium supports the growth of axenic strains such as Ax2 and AX4.
source: To generate fresh axenic strains for sequencing, we cultured wildtype D. discoideum cells in HL5 growth medium after washing them free of food bacteria. This medium supports the growth of axenic strains such as Ax2 and AX4, but wildtype cells arrest their growth and ultimately die.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the medium.

claim: Spontaneous mutants that are able to grow and proliferate in HL5 medium arise frequently among growth-arrested wildtype populations.
source: In order to minimize the number of irrelevant background mutations we avoided mutagenesis and found that spontaneous mutants that are able to grow and proliferate arise frequently among these growth-arrested populations.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: Three independent mutants were sequenced along with the parental DdB strain.
source: We selected several independent mutants and sequenced the genomes of three after clonal isolation, along with that of the parental DdB strain, which was chosen because it was also parent to the established axenic laboratory strains (Bloomfield et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: DdB was chosen as the parental strain because it was also parent to the established axenic laboratory strains.
source: We selected several independent mutants and sequenced the genomes of three after clonal isolation, along with that of the parental DdB strain, which was chosen because it was also parent to the established axenic laboratory strains (Bloomfield et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Only one mutation affecting coding sequence was initially identified in strain HM559 relative to the parent, a seven basepair deletion.
source: At first, other than two large duplications that do not correlate with axenicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we could only identify one mutation affecting coding sequence in any of these strains relative to their parent, a seven basepair deletion in strain HM559 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the genome sequencing analysis.

claim: Two large duplications were identified that do not correlate with axenicity.
source: At first, other than two large duplications that do not correlate with axenicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we could only identify one mutation affecting coding sequence in any of these strains relative to their parent, a seven basepair deletion in strain HM559 (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the genome sequencing analysis, with supporting figure.

claim: The reference genome sequence differs from its parent DdB in the same gene model (DDB_G0279251) as the mutation found in HM559.
source: We noted that the reference genome sequence (Eichinger et al., 2005), derived from the axenic mutant strain AX4, also differs from its parent DdB in the same gene model (annotated as DDB_G0279251).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing genome sequences.

claim: AX4 has lost almost nine kilobases of the NF1 gene region on chromosome 3, resulting in the deletion of most of the coding sequence.
source: Further analysis demonstrated that AX4 has lost almost nine kilobases of this region on chromosome 3, resulting in the deletion of most of the coding sequence of a large gene encoding a homologue of the Ras GTPase-activating protein (RasGAP) Neurofibromin (NF1), as well as part of the upstream gene (Figure 1A), with a short segment of extraneous sequence inserted.
evidence: This is a finding from genome sequence analysis, with supporting figure.

claim: The 7 bp deletion mutation in HM559 lies within the C-terminal region of the NF1 homologue.
source: The 7 bp deletion mutation in HM559 lies within the C-terminal region of this NF1 homologue, and we found that another established axenic mutant, Ax2, has exactly the same deletion-insertion mutation as AX4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, with supporting figure and table.

claim: Ax2 has exactly the same deletion-insertion mutation as AX4.
source: The 7 bp deletion mutation in HM559 lies within the C-terminal region of this NF1 homologue, and we found that another established axenic mutant, Ax2, has exactly the same deletion-insertion mutation as AX4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, with supporting figure and table.

claim: The ubiquity of mutations in the NF1 gene in axenic strains suggested that they must underlie the axenic phenotype.
source: The ubiquity of mutations in the NF1 gene in the axenic strains tested suggested that they must underlie the phenotype we selected for, and the gene's location on chromosome 3 accords with the mapping of the classically defined axeB gene (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between mutations and phenotype, supported by citation.

claim: The NF1 gene's location on chromosome 3 accords with the mapping of the classically defined axeB gene.
source: The ubiquity of mutations in the NF1 gene in the axenic strains tested suggested that they must underlie the phenotype we selected for, and the gene's location on chromosome 3 accords with the mapping of the classically defined axeB gene (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An engineered deletion of NF1 at the locus in wildtype strain DdB results in a mutant that is able to grow axenically in HL5 medium.
source: To test whether inactivation of NF1 promotes axenic growth, we engineered a deletion at the locus in a wildtype strain, DdB, and found that the resulting mutant is able to grow axenically in HL5 medium (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental manipulation, with supporting figure.

claim: The NF1 knockout mutant grows more slowly than the established Ax2 strain.
source: However, it grows more slowly than the established Ax2 strain (Figure 1B), and does not grow well in suspension in this medium (see below), confirming earlier findings that additional mutations are necessary to potentiate the basal axenic phenotype (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with supporting figure and citation.

claim: The NF1 knockout mutant does not grow well in suspension in HL5 medium.
source: However, it grows more slowly than the established Ax2 strain (Figure 1B), and does not grow well in suspension in this medium (see below), confirming earlier findings that additional mutations are necessary to potentiate the basal axenic phenotype (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with citation.

claim: Additional mutations are necessary to potentiate the basal axenic phenotype.
source: However, it grows more slowly than the established Ax2 strain (Figure 1B), and does not grow well in suspension in this medium (see below), confirming earlier findings that additional mutations are necessary to potentiate the basal axenic phenotype (Williams et al., 1974a, 1974b).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The identification of mutations in the original axenic strains on chromosome 3 and demonstration that inactivation of the affected gene results in a phenotype closely resembling axeB single mutants gives adequate reason to believe that the causative mutation has been identified.
source: Together, the identification of mutations in the original axenic strains on chromosome 3 and demonstration that inactivation of the affected gene results in a phenotype closely resembling axeB single mutants derived parasexually (Clarke and Kayman, 1987) gives adequate reason to believe that we have identified the original causative mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined evidence, with citation.

claim: The axeB locus is formally named for the gene encoding NF1.
source: We therefore formally retain the name axeB for the locus, while naming the encoded protein NF1.
evidence: This is a nomenclature decision based on the findings.

claim: The Dictyostelium NF1 gene encodes a protein with the same domain organization as the human version.
source: The Dictyostelium NF1 gene encodes a protein with the same domain organisation as the human version, with CRAL/TRIO and PH-like domains at the C-terminal side of the catalytic RasGAP domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, with supporting figure.

claim: The Dictyostelium NF1 protein is of a similar size to the human version.
source: It is also of a similar size, with homology extending across most of the two proteins' lengths (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, with supporting figure.

claim: The D. discoideum NF1 orthologue is about as similar to the human protein as are those from the basal metazoa and choanoflagellates.
source: The D. discoideum NF1 orthologue is about as similar to the human protein as are those from the basal metazoa and choanoflagellates (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence comparison, with supporting figure.

claim: NF1 is an ancient protein, conserved considerably beyond the metazoan and fungal lineages.
source: NF1 is an ancient protein, conserved considerably beyond the metazoan and fungal lineages in which it has been studied to date, with homologues in a variety of unicellular eukaryotes including the excavates Naegleria and Trichomonas as well as other amoebae (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Carlton et al., 2007; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010; Clarke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis, with supporting figures and citations.

claim: NF1 homologues are present in a variety of unicellular eukaryotes including the excavates Naegleria and Trichomonas as well as other amoebae.
source: NF1 is an ancient protein, conserved considerably beyond the metazoan and fungal lineages in which it has been studied to date, with homologues in a variety of unicellular eukaryotes including the excavates Naegleria and Trichomonas as well as other amoebae (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Carlton et al., 2007; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010; Clarke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis, with supporting figures and citations.

claim: RasGAPs are more broadly distributed than NF1, being present in further excavates as well as in certain ciliates, oomycetes, and the foraminiferan Reticulomyxa.
source: RasGAPs are more broadly distributed than NF1, being present in further excavates as well as in certain ciliates, oomycetes, and the foraminiferan Reticulomyxa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—source data 1; van Dam et al., 2011; Glöckner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis, with supporting figures and citations.

claim: The dictyostelids, Entamoeba, Thecamonas, and Naegleria all possess separate smaller homologues with a similar domain organization to NF1 but lacking homology outside of the central region, termed 'MNF' (for 'miniature neurofibromin').
source: The dictyostelids, Entamoeba, Thecamonas, and Naegleria all possess separate smaller homologues with a similar domain organisation to NF1 but lacking homology outside of the central region; we term these proteins 'MNF' (for 'miniature neurofibromin').
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis and a nomenclature decision.

claim: The D. discoideum NfaA protein falls into the MNF class.
source: The D. discoideum NfaA protein (Zhang et al., 2008) falls into this class (Figure 2A,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and is discussed further below.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis, with supporting figures and citation.

claim: The lysine to asparagine substitution occurring in one of the new axenic mutants has also been found in human cancer and Neurofibromatosis type 1 patients.
source: The lysine to asparagine substitution occurring in one of our new axenic mutants (see above) has also been found in human cancer and Neurofibromatosis type 1 patients (Li et al., 1992), and affects a lysine residue (numbered 1423 in the human polypeptide) that is located on the surface of the GAP domain where it contacts Ras, and that is essential for GAP activity (Poullet et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The lysine residue at position 1423 in the human NF1 polypeptide is located on the surface of the GAP domain where it contacts Ras and is essential for GAP activity.
source: The lysine to asparagine substitution occurring in one of our new axenic mutants (see above) has also been found in human cancer and Neurofibromatosis type 1 patients (Li et al., 1992), and affects a lysine residue (numbered 1423 in the human polypeptide) that is located on the surface of the GAP domain where it contacts Ras, and that is essential for GAP activity (Poullet et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The conservation of the critical lysine residue strikingly underscores the homology inferred from sequence analysis.
source: This strikingly underscores the homology inferred from sequence analysis, and furthermore suggests that overactivation of Ras subfamily small G proteins causes the axenic mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional conservation.

claim: Overactivation of Ras subfamily small G proteins causes the axenic mutant phenotype.
source: This strikingly underscores the homology inferred from sequence analysis, and furthermore suggests that overactivation of Ras subfamily small G proteins causes the axenic mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional conservation and known role of NF1.

claim: Established axenic mutants have very high rates of macropinocytosis.
source: Established axenic mutants have very high rates of macropinocytosis (Hacker et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When harvested directly from bacterial growth plates, NF1 mutants ingest fluid at about the same rate as Ax2, and more than four times more rapidly than wildtype cells.
source: When they are harvested directly from bacterial growth plates, NF1 mutants ingest fluid at about the same rate as an established axenic strain, Ax2, and more than four times more rapidly than wildtype cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with supporting figure.

claim: After prolonged incubation in HL5 medium without bacteria, Ax2 cells and NF1 mutants increase their fluid uptake further while wildtype cells decrease it.
source: After prolonged incubation in HL5 medium without bacteria, Ax2 cells and NF1 mutants increase their uptake further while wildtype cells decrease it, such that after 24 hr mutants take in fluid at a rate more than twenty times higher than the wildtype (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with supporting figure.

claim: After 24 hr in HL5 medium, mutants take in fluid at a rate more than twenty times higher than the wildtype.
source: After prolonged incubation in HL5 medium without bacteria, Ax2 cells and NF1 mutants increase their uptake further while wildtype cells decrease it, such that after 24 hr mutants take in fluid at a rate more than twenty times higher than the wildtype (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with supporting figure.

claim: Fluid uptake is linear at the earliest times measured with no evidence for rapid recycling of fluid in any of the strains.
source: Fluid uptake is linear at the earliest times measured with no evidence for rapid recycling of fluid in any of these strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), in agreement with earlier studies of axenic mutants (Aubry et al., 1993; Padh et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with supporting figure and citations.

claim: Membrane uptake measured using the accumulation of FM1-43 dye was not increased in NF1 mutants.
source: Membrane uptake measured using the accumulation of FM1-43 dye was not increased in NF1 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with an earlier comparison of Ax2 with wildtype cells (Aguado-Velasco and Bretscher, 1999).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data, with supporting figure and citation.

claim: Clathrin-dependent and -independent micropinocytotic processes in these cells are unaffected by NF1 loss.
source: Since this assay predominantly measures uptake into small vesicles or tubules with a high surface to volume ratio, we conclude that clathrin-dependent and -independent micropinocytotic processes in these cells (Neuhaus et al., 2002; Hirst et al., 2014), are unaffected by NF1 loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FM1-43 data, with citations.

claim: NF1 mutants accumulate large dextran-filled endosomes more prominently than wildtypes when bathed in fluorescent dextran.
source: When bathed in fluorescent dextran, NF1 mutants accumulate large dextran-filled endosomes more prominently than wildtypes (Figure 3B), consistent with the fluorimetry of cell populations.
evidence: This is a finding from confocal microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: NF1 mutants attached to glass coverslips tend to flatten periodically, a phenotype often observed in established axenic strains such as Ax2 but not in wildtype cells.
source: NF1 mutants attached to glass coverslips also tend to flatten periodically, a phenotype often observed in established axenic strains such as Ax2 but not in wildtype cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from confocal microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: In four-dimensional timelapse imaging, mutants perform macropinocytosis four times as frequently as wildtype cells.
source: In four-dimensional timelapse imaging, when freshly harvested from bacteria mutants and wildtype cells can be observed to enclose large macropinosomes after projecting cup- or crown-shaped ruffles, with the mutant performing macropinocytosis in this way four times as frequently as wildtype cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from confocal microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: The NF1 mutation accounts for the increased macropinocytotic fluid uptake of axenic strains.
source: The NF1 mutation therefore accounts for the increased macropinocytotic fluid uptake of axenic strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined experimental data.

claim: The NF1 knockout mutant grows more slowly than Ax2 despite taking in a similar amount of fluid.
source: Despite taking in a similar amount of fluid, the NF1 knockout mutant grows more slowly than Ax2 (see above).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Ax2 and the NF1 null strain rapidly and comparably degrade protein after internalization by macropinocytosis and maturation of endosomes.
source: Ax2 and the NF1 null strain rapidly and comparably degrade protein after internalization by macropinocytosis and maturation of endosomes, (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from DQ-BSA imaging, with supporting figure.

claim: Wildtype DdB cells effectively degrade DQ-BSA when taken freshly from bacterial growth but not after overnight incubation in axenic conditions.
source: Wildtype DdB cells effectively degrade DQ-BSA when taken freshly from bacterial growth but not after overnight incubation in axenic conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), again suggesting that they shut down endocytic feeding as part of a starvation response.
evidence: This is a finding from DQ-BSA imaging, with supporting figure.

claim: Wildtype cells shut down endocytic feeding as part of a starvation response.
source: Wildtype DdB cells effectively degrade DQ-BSA when taken freshly from bacterial growth but not after overnight incubation in axenic conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), again suggesting that they shut down endocytic feeding as part of a starvation response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DQ-BSA data.

claim: Deletion of the closely related MNF RasGAP, nfaA, from wildtype cells does not confer the ability to grow axenically.
source: First, we deleted the closely related MNF RasGAP, nfaA, from wildtype cells, and found that this does not confer the ability to grow axenically (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that NF1 has specific functions not shared by other GAPs.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental manipulation, with supporting figure.

claim: NF1 has specific functions not shared by other GAPs.
source: First, we deleted the closely related MNF RasGAP, nfaA, from wildtype cells, and found that this does not confer the ability to grow axenically (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that NF1 has specific functions not shared by other GAPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nfaA deletion data.

claim: NfaA has a distinct function regulating pseudopodium formation during chemotaxis.
source: This corroborates earlier findings that NfaA has a distinct function regulating pseudopodium formation during chemotaxis (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pulldowns of Ras-GTP from growing cells indicated no increase in Ras activity in mutants compared to wildtype cells.
source: Pulldowns of Ras-GTP using the Raf1 Ras-binding domain (RBD) from growing cells indicated no increase in Ras activity in mutants compared to wildtype cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from biochemical assays, with supporting figure.

claim: Confocal microscopy of cells expressing the GFP-RBD reporter revealed no difference between mutant and wildtypes in overall Ras activity estimated by determining the proportion the cell periphery labelled with the RBD.
source: Similarly, confocal microscopy of cells expressing the GFP-RBD reporter revealed no difference between mutant and wildtypes in overall Ras activity estimated by determining the proportion the cell periphery labelled with the RBD (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: NF1 is only one of twelve putative RasGAPs encoded in the D. discoideum genome.
source: This is not surprising, since NF1 is only one of twelve putative RasGAPs encoded in the D. discoideum genome (not including IQ-GAPs, which generally act as small G protein effectors and scaffolds and do not stimulate Ras GTPase activity [Shannon, 2012]).
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about the genome, with citation.

claim: In wildtypes, the GFP-RBD reporter is recruited intensely to small ruffles as they become concave and close into macropinosomes.
source: In wildtypes, as well as weak localisation at the leading edge of the cell, the GFP-RBD reporter is recruited intensely to small ruffles as they become concave and close into macropinosomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: In NF1 mutants, macropinocytotic ruffles tend to be larger than in wildtype cells.
source: In NF1 mutants, these specifically macropinocytotic ruffles tend to be larger (Figure 4A), 50% of them being greater than 2 µm across upon closure, compared to less than 10% in wildtype cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figures.

claim: 50% of macropinocytotic ruffles in NF1 mutants are greater than 2 µm across upon closure, compared to less than 10% in wildtype cells.
source: In NF1 mutants, these specifically macropinocytotic ruffles tend to be larger (Figure 4A), 50% of them being greater than 2 µm across upon closure, compared to less than 10% in wildtype cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy measurements, with supporting figure.

claim: Introduction of N-terminally GFP-tagged wildtype Dictyostelium NF1 protein into axeB mutants reduces axenic growth.
source: Introduction of N-terminally GFP-tagged Dictyostelium NF1 proteins into axeB mutants reduces axenic growth in the case of the wildtype sequence (NF1-WT) but not when two consecutive arginine residues in the protein's 'arginine finger' are mutated to alanine and serine (NF1-AS′), nor when only the central region of the protein encompassing the RasGAP, CRAL-TRIO, and PH-like domains (NF1ΔNΔC) is expressed, when compared to a GFP control.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental manipulation.

claim: Introduction of the NF1-AS mutant protein (with arginine finger mutated) into axeB mutants does not reduce axenic growth.
source: Introduction of N-terminally GFP-tagged Dictyostelium NF1 proteins into axeB mutants reduces axenic growth in the case of the wildtype sequence (NF1-WT) but not when two consecutive arginine residues in the protein's 'arginine finger' are mutated to alanine and serine (NF1-AS′), nor when only the central region of the protein encompassing the RasGAP, CRAL-TRIO, and PH-like domains (NF1ΔNΔC) is expressed, when compared to a GFP control.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental manipulation.

claim: Expression of only the central region of NF1 (NF1ΔNΔC) does not reduce axenic growth.
source: Introduction of N-terminally GFP-tagged Dictyostelium NF1 proteins into axeB mutants reduces axenic growth in the case of the wildtype sequence (NF1-WT) but not when two consecutive arginine residues in the protein's 'arginine finger' are mutated to alanine and serine (NF1-AS′), nor when only the central region of the protein encompassing the RasGAP, CRAL-TRIO, and PH-like domains (NF1ΔNΔC) is expressed, when compared to a GFP control.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental manipulation.

claim: The active NF1-RR construct almost completely abolishes macropinosome formation when expressed in NF1 mutants.
source: The active NF1-RR construct almost completely abolishes macropinosome formation when expressed in NF1 mutants, while the inactive NF1-AS form does not inhibit macropinocytosis.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy of expressing cells.

claim: The inactive NF1-AS form does not inhibit macropinocytosis.
source: The active NF1-RR construct almost completely abolishes macropinosome formation when expressed in NF1 mutants, while the inactive NF1-AS form does not inhibit macropinocytosis.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy of expressing cells.

claim: The NF1-AS mutant protein is recruited to membrane ruffles and sites of macropinocytosis.
source: The NF1-AS mutant protein is recruited to membrane ruffles and sites of macropinocytosis (examples indicated by pointers), whereas the wildtype version (NF1-RR) has an even cytoplasmic distribution, as does the truncated NF1ΔNΔC protein.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy of expressing cells.

claim: The wildtype NF1-RR protein has an even cytoplasmic distribution.
source: The NF1-AS mutant protein is recruited to membrane ruffles and sites of macropinocytosis (examples indicated by pointers), whereas the wildtype version (NF1-RR) has an even cytoplasmic distribution, as does the truncated NF1ΔNΔC protein.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy of expressing cells.

claim: The truncated NF1ΔNΔC protein has an even cytoplasmic distribution.
source: The NF1-AS mutant protein is recruited to membrane ruffles and sites of macropinocytosis (examples indicated by pointers), whereas the wildtype version (NF1-RR) has an even cytoplasmic distribution, as does the truncated NF1ΔNΔC protein.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy of expressing cells.

claim: Other regions of the NF1 protein are required for its correct localization.
source: Since the spontaneous inversion mutation we identified (Table 1) affects the C-terminal region of the protein, we also tested whether the core RasGAP-Sec14-PH region of the D. discoideum NF1 protein could rescue the NF1 mutant; like the NF-AS version this did not suppress axenic growth (Figure 4C), and displayed an evenly cytosolic distribution (Figure 4E), suggesting that other regions of the protein are required for its correct localisation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data.

claim: The inactive NF1-AS form of the protein is presumably recruited by strong Ras activity at macropinocytotic crowns that it is then unable to attenuate.
source: The inactive NF1-AS form of the protein is presumably recruited by strong Ras activity at macropinocytotic crowns that it is then unable to attenuate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and activity data.

claim: NF1 directly regulates signaling at the plasma membrane during ruffling.
source: This localisation implies that the NF1 protein directly regulates signalling at the plasma membrane during ruffling, and together with the more extensive Ras signalling during macropinocytosis, suggests that this RasGAP regulates a pool of Ras responsible for this feeding process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data.

claim: NF1 regulates a pool of Ras responsible for macropinocytosis.
source: This localisation implies that the NF1 protein directly regulates signalling at the plasma membrane during ruffling, and together with the more extensive Ras signalling during macropinocytosis, suggests that this RasGAP regulates a pool of Ras responsible for this feeding process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data.

claim: Two Dictyostelium Ras proteins have been linked to endocytic functions.
source: Two Dictyostelium Ras proteins have been linked to endocytic functions (Chubb et al., 2000; Hoeller et al., 2013); to examine their involvement in NF1-controlled events we expressed GFP-tagged versions of each in NF1 mutant and wildtype cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All tested GFP-tagged Ras constructs localized to the plasma membrane, except for dominant negative (S17N mutant) RasG and RasS.
source: All tested GFP-tagged Ras constructs localised to the plasma membrane, except for dominant negative (S17N mutant) RasG and RasS, expression of which was apparently poorly tolerated in these strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: None of the Dictyostelium Ras expression constructs phenocopied the loss of NF1.
source: None of the Dictyostelium Ras expression constructs phenocopied the loss of NF1; constitutively active RasG was deleterious to growth, as was expression of wildtype or constitutively active RasS (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that improper activation of these isoforms interferes with endocytosis or other Ras-influenced processes leading to detrimental effects on cell growth.
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figure.

claim: Constitutively active RasG was deleterious to growth.
source: None of the Dictyostelium Ras expression constructs phenocopied the loss of NF1; constitutively active RasG was deleterious to growth, as was expression of wildtype or constitutively active RasS (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that improper activation of these isoforms interferes with endocytosis or other Ras-influenced processes leading to detrimental effects on cell growth.
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figure.

claim: Expression of wildtype or constitutively active RasS was deleterious to growth.
source: None of the Dictyostelium Ras expression constructs phenocopied the loss of NF1; constitutively active RasG was deleterious to growth, as was expression of wildtype or constitutively active RasS (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that improper activation of these isoforms interferes with endocytosis or other Ras-influenced processes leading to detrimental effects on cell growth.
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figure.

claim: Improper activation of RasG or RasS isoforms interferes with endocytosis or other Ras-influenced processes leading to detrimental effects on cell growth.
source: None of the Dictyostelium Ras expression constructs phenocopied the loss of NF1; constitutively active RasG was deleterious to growth, as was expression of wildtype or constitutively active RasS (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that improper activation of these isoforms interferes with endocytosis or other Ras-influenced processes leading to detrimental effects on cell growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth data.

claim: Ras activity at membrane ruffles in NF1 mutants is accompanied by recruitment of PH-domain reporters that bind the plasmanyl inositides produced by Dictyostelium class 1 PI3Ks.
source: Confirming that the macropinosomes observed in NF1 mutants are mechanistically similar to those previously documented, we find that Ras activity at membrane ruffles in NF1 mutants is accompanied by recruitment of PH-domain reporters that bind the plasmanyl inositides produced by Dictyostelium class 1 PI3Ks (Figure 5A; Clark et al., 2014), as well as by actin polymerisation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figures and citation.

claim: Ras activity at membrane ruffles in NF1 mutants is accompanied by actin polymerization.
source: Confirming that the macropinosomes observed in NF1 mutants are mechanistically similar to those previously documented, we find that Ras activity at membrane ruffles in NF1 mutants is accompanied by recruitment of PH-domain reporters that bind the plasmanyl inositides produced by Dictyostelium class 1 PI3Ks (Figure 5A; Clark et al., 2014), as well as by actin polymerisation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: PH domains are prominently recruited during macropinocytosis in wildtype cells.
source: PH domains are also prominently recruited during macropinocytosis in wildtype cells; regions of recruitment tend to be larger in mutants reflecting the increased Ras signalling that results from the absence of NF1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: Regions of PH domain recruitment tend to be larger in mutants reflecting the increased Ras signaling that results from the absence of NF1.
source: PH domains are also prominently recruited during macropinocytosis in wildtype cells; regions of recruitment tend to be larger in mutants reflecting the increased Ras signalling that results from the absence of NF1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: The pattern of Ras activity and PIP3 formation is invariably observed in every instance of macropinocytosis in Dictyostelium.
source: This pattern of Ras activity and PIP3 formation is invariably observed in every instance of macropinocytosis in Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: No increase in ERK activity is observed in NF1 mutants compared to wildtype cells.
source: The contributions of other Ras effectors remain unclear; for example no increase in ERK activity is observed in NF1 mutants compared to wildtype cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting, with supporting figure.

claim: Wildtype cells are able to grow in HL5 medium supplemented with foetal bovine serum.
source: Wildtype cells incubated in stationary cultures in HL5 supplemented with foetal bovine serum (or bovine serum albumin, data not shown) were able to grow, albeit still much more slowly than NF1 mutants cultured in the same medium (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figures.

claim: Wildtype cells grow much more slowly than NF1 mutants in HL5 supplemented with serum.
source: Wildtype cells incubated in stationary cultures in HL5 supplemented with foetal bovine serum (or bovine serum albumin, data not shown) were able to grow, albeit still much more slowly than NF1 mutants cultured in the same medium (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figures.

claim: The morphology of wildtype cells was not appreciably altered after several days of axenic growth in serum-supplemented medium.
source: The morphology of wildtype cells was not appreciably altered after several days of axenic growth, while NF1 mutants remained consistently more flattened and extensively ruffled than wildtype cells in the same conditions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: NF1 mutants remained consistently more flattened and extensively ruffled than wildtype cells in serum-supplemented medium.
source: The morphology of wildtype cells was not appreciably altered after several days of axenic growth, while NF1 mutants remained consistently more flattened and extensively ruffled than wildtype cells in the same conditions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: Wildtype cells degrade DQ-BSA efficiently after axenic growth in the presence of serum.
source: Wildtype cells were also found to degrade DQ-BSA efficiently after axenic growth in the presence of serum (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure.

claim: Serum addition stimulated the growth of NF1 mutants in shaking suspension.
source: Serum addition also stimulated the growth of NF1 mutants in shaking suspension (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figure.

claim: The additional nutrients in serum-supplemented broth allow wildtype cells to avoid the starvation-triggered growth arrest that can occur in axenic media.
source: These findings suggest that the additional nutrients in the richer broth allow these cells to avoid the starvation-triggered growth arrest that can occur in axenic media.
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth data.

claim: Mutant and wildtype strains grow well on bacteria.
source: Finally, since macropinocytosis and phagocytosis are closely related processes we compared phagocytosis in NF1 mutants and wildtype cells. Mutant and wildtype strains grow well on bacteria (Figure 7—figure supplements 1, 2) and take up bacterium-sized polystyrene microspheres (1 μm and 1.8 μm diameter) at very similar rates (Figure 7A), although the standard strain Ax2 is marginally but consistently less effective at internalising smaller beads than the other strains (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays, with supporting figures.

claim: Mutant and wildtype strains take up bacterium-sized polystyrene microspheres (1 μm and 1.8 μm diameter) at very similar rates.
source: Finally, since macropinocytosis and phagocytosis are closely related processes we compared phagocytosis in NF1 mutants and wildtype cells. Mutant and wildtype strains grow well on bacteria (Figure 7—figure supplements 1, 2) and take up bacterium-sized polystyrene microspheres (1 μm and 1.8 μm diameter) at very similar rates (Figure 7A), although the standard strain Ax2 is marginally but consistently less effective at internalising smaller beads than the other strains (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from phagocytosis assays, with supporting figure.

claim: Ax2 is marginally but consistently less effective at internalizing smaller beads than the other strains.
source: Finally, since macropinocytosis and phagocytosis are closely related processes we compared phagocytosis in NF1 mutants and wildtype cells. Mutant and wildtype strains grow well on bacteria (Figure 7—figure supplements 1, 2) and take up bacterium-sized polystyrene microspheres (1 μm and 1.8 μm diameter) at very similar rates (Figure 7A), although the standard strain Ax2 is marginally but consistently less effective at internalising smaller beads than the other strains (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from phagocytosis assays, with supporting figure.

claim: Wildtype cells cannot efficiently ingest yeast or beads greater than 3 μm in diameter.
source: Against expectation, we found that wildtype cells cannot efficiently ingest yeast or beads greater than 3 μm in diameter (Figure 7A,C), whereas NF1 mutant cells can ingest beads larger than 4 μm in diameter (Figure 7A) or yeast cells very readily (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from phagocytosis assays, with supporting figures.

claim: NF1 mutant cells can ingest beads larger than 4 μm in diameter.
source: Against expectation, we found that wildtype cells cannot efficiently ingest yeast or beads greater than 3 μm in diameter (Figure 7A,C), whereas NF1 mutant cells can ingest beads larger than 4 μm in diameter (Figure 7A) or yeast cells very readily (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from phagocytosis assays, with supporting figures.

claim: NF1 mutant cells can ingest yeast cells very readily.
source: Against expectation, we found that wildtype cells cannot efficiently ingest yeast or beads greater than 3 μm in diameter (Figure 7A,C), whereas NF1 mutant cells can ingest beads larger than 4 μm in diameter (Figure 7A) or yeast cells very readily (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from phagocytosis assays, with supporting figures.

claim: RBD and PH domain reporters localized to phagosomes as they formed, essentially identically to their behavior during macropinocytosis.
source: In line with earlier findings in Ax2 cells (Clarke et al., 2010), RBD and PH domain reporters localised to phagosomes as they formed, essentially identically to their behaviour during macropinocytosis (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy, with supporting figure and citation.

claim: NF1 limits the size of nascent phagosomes.
source: We conclude that, as well as controlling macropinocytosis, NF1 limits the size of nascent phagosomes, supporting the idea that these large-scale endocytic processes share regulatory as well as structural features.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phagocytosis data.

claim: Large-scale endocytic processes share regulatory as well as structural features.
source: We conclude that, as well as controlling macropinocytosis, NF1 limits the size of nascent phagosomes, supporting the idea that these large-scale endocytic processes share regulatory as well as structural features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data.

claim: Variation in or loss of NF1 can have important ecological and evolutionary consequences by enabling predators to target additional prey species.
source: The striking improvement in phagocytosis of larger cells after NF1 deletion also suggests that variation in or loss of this gene can have important ecological and evolutionary consequences by enabling predators to target additional prey species (Porter, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the phagocytosis data, with citation.

claim: The identification of axeB as NF1 will provide a route towards creating new axenic strains from wild isolates.
source: Our identification of the axeB gene as NF1 will provide a route towards creating new axenic strains from wild isolates, thus giving strains with minimal background mutations.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claim: Vegetative wildtype cells perform macropinocytosis in a qualitatively similar way as axenic mutants but to a lesser extent.
source: Vegetative wildtype cells perform macropinocytosis in a qualitatively similar way as axenic mutants but to a lesser extent, and accordingly they can grow axenically when the standard medium is supplemented with bovine serum.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data.

claim: NF1 mutants retain a large growth advantage in serum-supplemented medium.
source: NF1 mutants retain a large growth advantage in the more complex medium, and so will still be selected during prolonged culture.
evidence: This is an observation from the growth data.

claim: Standard defined medium supplemented with bovine serum albumin enables slow growth of wildtype strains.
source: Nevertheless, this protocol should be of use for short-term axenic culture of wildtype strains; standard defined medium supplemented with bovine serum albumin also enables slow growth of wildtype strains (unpublished data) suggesting that fully synthetic defined media should be attainable.
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data.

claim: Fully synthetic defined media for wildtype Dictyostelium should be attainable.
source: Nevertheless, this protocol should be of use for short-term axenic culture of wildtype strains; standard defined medium supplemented with bovine serum albumin also enables slow growth of wildtype strains (unpublished data) suggesting that fully synthetic defined media should be attainable.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the growth data.

claim: The important effect of serum is the provision of bulk nutrients, preventing the nitrogen starvation that initiates Dictyostelium development.
source: This further supports the idea that the important effect of serum is the provision of bulk nutrients, preventing the nitrogen starvation that initiates Dictyostelium development (Marin, 1976).
evidence: This is an inference based on the growth data, with citation.

claim: Key roles for Ras and PIP3 in steering migrating cells have been proposed.
source: One important focus of Dictyostelium research is chemotaxis, and key roles for Ras and PIP3 in steering migrating cells have been proposed (Kay et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Axenic cells are much less efficient than wildtype cells in chemotaxis to folic acid, due to interference from large, PIP3-rich, macropinosomes.
source: Although axenic cells chemotax very well to the best-studied chemoattractant, cyclic-AMP, they are much less efficient than wildtype cells in chemotaxis to folic acid, due to interference from large, PIP3-rich, macropinosomes (Veltman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The reason for poor chemotaxis to folic acid in axenic cells is likely to be the inactivation of NF1 in axenic cells, leading to Ras and PI3K hyperactivity.
source: It is now apparent that the reason for this poor chemotaxis is likely to be the inactivation of NF1 in axenic cells, leading to Ras and PI3K hyperactivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of this study.

claim: Macropinosomes and intense patches of Ras activity and PIP3 appear in cells chemotaxing to cyclic-AMP.
source: Macropinosomes and intense patches of Ras activity and PIP3 also appear in cells chemotaxing to cyclic-AMP (Parent et al., 1998) and it will be important to disentangle their contribution to chemotaxis by comparative studies of axenic and wildtype cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: It will be important to disentangle the contribution of macropinosomes to chemotaxis by comparative studies of axenic and wildtype cells.
source: Macropinosomes and intense patches of Ras activity and PIP3 also appear in cells chemotaxing to cyclic-AMP (Parent et al., 1998) and it will be important to disentangle their contribution to chemotaxis by comparative studies of axenic and wildtype cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Previous studies in Dictyostelium showed defects in macropinocytosis and phagocytosis after disruption of Ras genes.
source: Several lines of evidence emphasize the importance of Ras in the feeding process used by Dictyostelium cells. Previous studies in Dictyostelium showed defects in macropinocytosis and phagocytosis after disruption of Ras genes (Chubb et al., 2000; Hoeller et al., 2013), and Ras activates PI3K during macropinocytosis (Hoeller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ras activates PI3K during macropinocytosis.
source: Several lines of evidence emphasize the importance of Ras in the feeding process used by Dictyostelium cells. Previous studies in Dictyostelium showed defects in macropinocytosis and phagocytosis after disruption of Ras genes (Chubb et al., 2000; Hoeller et al., 2013), and Ras activates PI3K during macropinocytosis (Hoeller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ras activity reporters localize strongly to membrane ruffles during macropinocytosis as well as to nascent phagosomes.
source: Further, Ras activity reporters localise strongly to membrane ruffles during macropinocytosis as well as to nascent phagosomes (Sasaki et al., 2007; Clarke et al., 2010), and we found that the size of these sites of Ras activity is increased in NF1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and the current study's data.

claim: The well-studied NF1 orthologues in mammals and yeast are specific to Ras subfamily small G proteins.
source: The well-studied NF1 orthologues in mammals and yeast are specific to Ras subfamily small G proteins (Tanaka et al., 1990; Zhang et al., 1991), and one of mutations we found in Dictyostelium corresponds exactly to one that abolishes the GAP activity of the human orthologue by altering the Ras-binding interface of the protein (Poullet et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dictyostelium NF1 is most likely Ras-specific.
source: These data, along with the effect of mutating the 'arginine finger' critical for RasGAP activity, suggest that Dictyostelium NF1 is most likely Ras-specific, but this remains to be demonstrated biochemically.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data, but noted as requiring biochemical confirmation.

claim: The specificity of Dictyostelium NF1 towards different Ras isoforms remains unclear.
source: The specificity of Dictyostelium NF1 towards different Ras isoforms remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Multiple Ras isoforms are likely involved in endocytic feeding in Dictyostelium.
source: Since the rasG and rasS null mutants have defective endocytic feeding but are still viable (Chubb et al., 2000; Hoeller et al., 2013) it is likely that multiple Ras isoforms are involved, possibly including other less well-characterised genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous literature.

claim: A module comprising a CRAL/TRIO and a PH-like domain is conserved in NF1 and likely mediates an interaction with lipids within cells.
source: A module comprising a CRAL/TRIO and a PH-like domain is conserved and likely mediates an interaction with lipids within cells (D'angelo et al., 2006), but has not been tied to any function of consequence.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The CRAL/TRIO and PH-like domain module has not been tied to any function of consequence.
source: A module comprising a CRAL/TRIO and a PH-like domain is conserved and likely mediates an interaction with lipids within cells (D'angelo et al., 2006), but has not been tied to any function of consequence.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Regions of conserved sequence to either side of the core of the NF1 protein may be important for its function in Dictyostelium, perhaps by mediating its dynamic localization.
source: Regions of conserved sequence to either side of the relatively well-characterised core of the protein are even more mysterious, but may be important for its function in Dictyostelium, perhaps by mediating its dynamic localisation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the localization data.

claim: GFP-tagged full length Dictyostelium NF1 localizes transiently to macropinocytotic ruffles.
source: We find that GFP-tagged full length Dictyostelium NF1 localises transiently to macropinocytotic ruffles.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy.

claim: Over-expression of the active NF1 protein almost completely inhibits macropinocytosis.
source: This translocation has only been visualised in a mutant form of the protein with the 'arginine finger' motif mutated, because over-expression of the active protein almost completely inhibits macropinocytosis.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy.

claim: It will be important to identify structural determinants of NF1 localization as a route towards a better understanding of the cell-biological function of NF1.
source: It will be important to identify structural determinants of this localisation as a route towards a better understanding of the cell-biological function of NF1.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: NF1 stimulates Ras GTPase activity as endocytic ruffles form and spread, thereby limiting their size.
source: Both macropinosomes and phagosomes are significantly larger in NF1 mutants than in wildtypes, suggesting that NF1 stimulates Ras GTPase activity as endocytic ruffles form and spread, thereby limiting their size (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data, with supporting figure.

claim: The control of NF1 function is not well understood.
source: The control of NF1 function is not well understood, but our results suggest that it might be locally inactivated during macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge.

claim: NF1 might be locally inactivated during macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
source: The control of NF1 function is not well understood, but our results suggest that it might be locally inactivated during macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Growth factor treatment of mammalian cells leads to rapid degradation of NF1 by the proteasome.
source: In an intriguing parallel, growth factor treatment of mammalian cells leads to rapid degradation of NF1 by the proteasome (Cichowski et al., 2003) and also triggers membrane ruffling and macropinocytosis with similar kinetics (Brunk et al., 1976; Mellström et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Growth factor treatment of mammalian cells triggers membrane ruffling and macropinocytosis with similar kinetics to NF1 degradation.
source: In an intriguing parallel, growth factor treatment of mammalian cells leads to rapid degradation of NF1 by the proteasome (Cichowski et al., 2003) and also triggers membrane ruffling and macropinocytosis with similar kinetics (Brunk et al., 1976; Mellström et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No obvious fluid-uptake phenotype was found in NF1 null mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: However, we could find no obvious fluid-uptake phenotype in NF1 null mouse embryonic fibroblasts, suggesting that NF1 inactivation is not sufficient for stimulation of macropinocytosis in these cells (unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data.

claim: NF1 inactivation is not sufficient for stimulation of macropinocytosis in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: However, we could find no obvious fluid-uptake phenotype in NF1 null mouse embryonic fibroblasts, suggesting that NF1 inactivation is not sufficient for stimulation of macropinocytosis in these cells (unpublished data).
evidence: This is an inference based on unpublished data.

claim: The possibility remains that NF1 function is conserved in metazoa, but in a context in which Ras activity is more heavily regulated.
source: Given the known involvement of Ras signalling in promoting ruffling and macropinocytosis the possibility remains that NF1 function is conserved in metazoa, but in a context in which Ras activity is more heavily regulated, with additional layers of control not present in amoebae (Casci et al., 1999; Johnson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and previous literature.

claim: The set of species possessing NF1 homologues indicates the extreme antiquity of this protein.
source: The set of species possessing NF1 homologues indicates the extreme antiquity of this protein: NF1 is present in the excavates Naegleria and Trichomonas as well as the amoebae, animals, and fungi.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Recent placements of the root of the eukaryotes within the excavate group suggest that NF1 evolved very early in the history of eukaryotes.
source: Recent placements of the root of the eukaryotes within the excavate group (He et al., 2014; Derelle et al., 2015) suggest that NF1 evolved very early in the history of eukaryotes, and may have been present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA), along with the related protein MNF.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis and citations.

claim: NF1 may have been present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA).
source: Recent placements of the root of the eukaryotes within the excavate group (He et al., 2014; Derelle et al., 2015) suggest that NF1 evolved very early in the history of eukaryotes, and may have been present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA), along with the related protein MNF.
evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The hypothesis is proposed that NF1 and MNF evolved together to control the movements of the exploratory cell projections used in very early eukaryotes during feeding.
source: The presence of these RasGAPs in organisms that display strikingly similar forms of circular ruffling suggests the hypothesis that NF1 and MNF evolved together to control the movements of the exploratory cell projections used in very early eukaryotes during feeding (Boschek et al., 1981; John et al., 1984; Hacker et al., 1997; Cavalier-Smith, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic analysis and functional data, with citations.

claim: Macropinocytosis and phagocytosis occur in a well-defined series of stages that are shared between amoebae and vertebrate cells.
source: Macropinocytosis and phagocytosis occur in a well-defined series of stages that are shared between amoebae and vertebrate cells (Swanson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is used to project membrane ruffles outwards to enclose either a bound particle or extracellular fluid.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is used to project membrane ruffles outwards to enclose either a bound particle or extracellular fluid, inositol phospholipids accumulate and are then dephosphorylated in a well-defined sequence (Dormann et al., 2004; Egami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inositol phospholipids accumulate and are then dephosphorylated in a well-defined sequence during macropinocytosis and phagocytosis.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is used to project membrane ruffles outwards to enclose either a bound particle or extracellular fluid, inositol phospholipids accumulate and are then dephosphorylated in a well-defined sequence (Dormann et al., 2004; Egami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ras has previously been implicated in macropinocytosis and phagocytosis in Dictyostelium.
source: The role of Ras is less well understood, but has previously been implicated in macropinocytosis and phagocytosis in Dictyostelium (Chubb et al., 2000; Hoeller et al., 2013), and in circular ruffle formation, macropinocytosis, and trogocytosis in vertebrate cells (Bar-Sagi and Feramisco, 1986; Martínez-Martín et al., 2011; Welliver and Swanson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ras has been implicated in circular ruffle formation, macropinocytosis, and trogocytosis in vertebrate cells.
source: The role of Ras is less well understood, but has previously been implicated in macropinocytosis and phagocytosis in Dictyostelium (Chubb et al., 2000; Hoeller et al., 2013), and in circular ruffle formation, macropinocytosis, and trogocytosis in vertebrate cells (Bar-Sagi and Feramisco, 1986; Martínez-Martín et al., 2011; Welliver and Swanson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The unbiased forward genetic analysis suggests that NF1 has a fundamental role in governing the feeding processes used by amoebae.
source: Our unbiased forward genetic analysis suggests that NF1 has a fundamental role in governing the feeding processes used by amoebae.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The mechanistic parallels between large-scale endocytosis in metazoa and amoebae, as well as their shared history, raise the possibility that NF1 function is conserved.
source: The mechanistic parallels between large-scale endocytosis in metazoa and amoebae, as well as their shared history, raise the possibility that this function is conserved.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The role of Schwann cells as non-professional phagocytes during the repair of nerve damage is striking in the context of NF1 function.
source: The role of Schwann cells, the cell-type of origin of neurofibromas, as non-professional phagocytes during the repair of nerve damage (Stoll et al., 1989) is striking in this regard.
evidence: This is an observation connecting the findings to previous literature.

claim: The cell-biological function of NF1 is still not well understood.
source: Although the consequences of NF1 mutation are well understood in humans, its cell-biological function is still not well understood (Stephen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of knowledge, with citation.

claim: The results linking NF1 to macropinocytosis and phagocytosis may provide an important clue to understanding NF1's cell-biological function.
source: Our results, for the first time linking NF1 to macropinocytosis and phagocytosis, may provide an important clue.
evidence: This is a speculation about the significance of the findings.
